newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-South Korea's POSCO sees big ore demand rise.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-South Korea's POSCO sees big ore demand rise.

text.p: South Korea's Pohang Iron and Steel Co Ltd (POSCO), the world's second largest steelmaker, will have a greatly increased annual demand of 37.5 million tonnes of iron ore by 2000, Jin Tae Moh, manager and chief executive iron ore purchasing division, said on Thursday.
Addressing an industry conference here, Moh said full production at the group's fifth blast furnace would increase year 2000 iron ore demand by 3.7 million tonnes from 1996.
The new blast furnace would operate without need for an additional coke oven and a sinter plant, bringing substantial changes in POSCO's iron ore consumption pattern, he said.
POSCO plans to make up for the sintered ore shortage with pellets by doubling pellet consumption to 4.5 million tonnes in year 2000 from 2.2 million tonnes in 1996, he said.

This would increase pellet usage to about 12.0 percent of total iron ore consumption in year 2000 from 6.4 percent in 1996, he said. Australia would continue to be one of the most important suppliers to POSCO, he said.

Changing requirements would involve more emphasis on iron ore quality as well as rapid increases in requirements for steel scrap and hot briquetted iron (HBI) to about four million tonnes a year by this year, he said.

Australia supplies about 50 percent of POSCO's annual imported iron ore, which reached 34.1 million tonnes last year after rising from just 1.4 million tonnes 23 years ago. POSCO increased purchases of Australian iron ore to more than 17 million tonnes in 1996 from just 646,000 in 1974, he said.

A big increase in pellet requirements and the need for stable sources of high quality pellet were the reasons why the company established a joint-venture pellet plant with iron ore producer Companhia Valedo Rio Doce of Brazil, he said.
This has an annual production capacity of four million tonnes, for commissioning in mid-1988.
POSCO plans to take about 2.3 million tonners a year from the joint-venture plant, with the other half of total requirements to be purchased from varied sources under long-term contracts, he said.

POSCO's demand for steel scrap and substitutes, would increase drastically to about four million tonnes a year from about 1.8 million tonnes in 1996, beginning in 1997, with commissioning of a mini-mill, he said. Most will be imported.
POSCO's entry as a shareholder in the 1.5 million tonne a year Venezuela HBI venture, to begin production next month, was undertaken to stabilise the supply of metallics, Moh said.

POSCO's present steelmaking capacity is 23.8 million tonnes, with 21.2 million produced by blast furnace and 2.6 million by electric arc furnace. Total capacity is expected to rise to about 28 million tonnes in early 1999, Moh said.

The company produces about 60 percent of South Korea's total steel production, with POSCO's 1997 crude steel production forecast to rise to 26.5 million tonnes, up by 2.2 million tonnes on the year before.
South Korea's total crude steel production reached 39.0 million tonnes in 1996, up six percent on 1995.
Nippon Steel Corp of Japan is the world's biggest steel producer in terms of crude steel output.
